 1 TO ALL PARTIES AND TO THEIR COUNSEL OF RECORD:

 2          PLEASE TAKE NOTICE THAT, on December 11, 2025 at 9:00 a.m., or as soon thereafter

 3 as the matter may be heard in the Courtroom of the Honorable Edward J. Davila (Courtroom 4) of

 4 the above-entitled Court, located at 280 South 1st Street, San Jose, CA 95113, defendant SMIC,

 5 AMERICAS (“Americas”) will and hereby does move this Court to dismiss the Complaint

 6 (“Complt.”) filed by plaintiff High Sharp Electronic Limited (“Plaintiff”) pursuant to Federal Rules

 7 of Civil Procedure (“Rules”) 8(a) and 12(b)(6).

 8          This Motion is made on the grounds that Plaintiff has failed to state any claims against

 9 Americas. It is based on this Notice of Motion, the attached Memorandum of Points and Authorities,

10 the Joint Request for Judicial Notice and Incorporation by Reference (“JRJN”) concurrently filed

11 by defendants Semiconductor Manufacturing International Corporation (“SMIC”)                       and

12 Semiconductor Manufacturing South China Corporation (“SMSC”), all of the pleadings, files, and

13 records in this proceeding, and any other argument or evidence that may be presented to or

14 considered by the Court.

15                             CIVIL L.R. 3-4 STATEMENT OF ISSUES

16          1.      Whether Plaintiff can plausibly plead that Americas and defendants SMIC and

17 SMSC are alter egos of one another without any facts whatsoever to establish either that: (a) failure

18 to disregard the separate identities would result in fraud or injustice; or (b) there is such unity of

19 interest and ownership that the separate personalities of these entities no longer exist?

20          2.      Whether Plaintiff can state a claim against Americas based on indiscriminate group

21 pleading and allegations making clear Americas had no involvement in the purported semiconductor

22 wafer sales transaction?

23          3.      Whether Plaintiff can assert a claim under the United Nations Convention on

24 Contracts for the International Sale of Goods (“UNCISG”) against Americas when Americas’ place

25 of business is admittedly in the same Contracting State (i.e., signatory nation) as Plaintiff’s?

26          4.      Whether Plaintiff can pursue a conversion claim when the 3-year statute of
27 limitations on such claim has run?

          Case 5:25-cv-04605-EJD         Document 35       Filed 08/22/25      Page 7 of 17




 1                         MEMORANDUM OF POINTS AND AUTHORITIES

 2 I.         INTRODUCTION

 3            In Footnote 1 of the Complaint, Plaintiff acknowledges that it has refiled in this Court an

 4 action styled High Sharp Electronic Limited v. Semiconductor Manufacturing South China

 5 Corporation et al., No. 2:23-cv-08934-CAS-AGRx (C.D. Cal., filed Oct. 23, 2023) that it had

 6 previously pursued against SMIC, SMSC, and certain individual defendants in the Central District

 7 of California (“CD Cal. Case”). See Complt. ¶1 n.1. However, Plaintiff conspicuously omits from

 8 this footnote all of the following facts that give the lie to its assertion that it voluntarily dismissed

 9 the CD Cal. Case because the Northern District “was the most appropriate venue,” and reveal that,

10 Plaintiff was and is simply maneuvering to escape Judge Snyder’s rulings against it:

11            (1)    Plaintiff insisted in the CD. Cal. Case that: (a) all of the wrongdoing and harm

12            it had suffered had occurred in the Central District; and (b) it did not even know that

13            Americas existed until around August 27, 2024, years after the subject wafer deal

14            was allegedly entered into around November 15, 2021, and then breached in early

15            2022 (see JRJN1 Ex. B – CD Cal. Case Dkt. 1 ¶¶4-6, 9, 34-43]; JRJN Ex. D – CD

16            Cal. Case Dkt. 34 at 4, 6 (responding to Judge Snyder’s August 7, 2024 OSC re Lack

17            of Prosecution by explaining that, in the face of the OSC, its “Counsel researched

18            and located a potential address for SMIC in California”));

19            (2)    Judge Snyder granted SMSC’s motion to dismiss to the extent based on

20            insufficient service because, inter alia, Plaintiff’s “contention that [SMSC, SMIC

21            and Americas] are ‘one and the same’” notwithstanding, Plaintiff had failed to

22            establish through its allegations and evidence that there was “a sufficiently close

23            connection between these three entities” to enable service on SMSC through service

24
     1
25       The CD Cal. Case filings referenced herein are attached to the JRJN, and may be considered on

26 this motion to dismiss. See Fed. R. Evid. 201(b); Harris v. Cnty. of Orange, 682 F.3d 1126, 1132
27 (9th Cir. 2012) (“We may take judicial notice of undisputed matters of public record, including

28 documents on file in federal or state courts.”) (internal citations omitted).
                                                   1                        Case No. 5:25-cv-04605
                        SMIC, AMERICAS’ NOTICE OF MOTION AND MOTION TO DISMISS;
                                MEMORANDUM OF POINTS AND AUTHORITIES
          Case 5:25-cv-04605-EJD        Document 35       Filed 08/22/25     Page 8 of 17




 1            on Americas (see JRJN Ex. A – CD Cal. Case Dkt. 61 at 12-14);

 2            (3)    In ruling on SMIC’s concurrently filed motion to dismiss based on lack of

 3            personal jurisdiction,2 Judge Snyder similarly found Plaintiff’s allegations and

 4            evidence fell short of establishing personal jurisdiction over SMIC, including as

 5            Americas’ alter ego (see id. at 16-17);

 6            (4)    Plaintiff repeatedly requested jurisdictional discovery to establish SMIC and

 7            Americas “are effectively one and the same,” but when Judge Snyder gave it the

 8            opportunity to engage in such discovery and reargue the availability of personal

 9            jurisdiction as to SMIC, Plaintiff (knowing full well that such discovery would not

10            actually aid its position) voluntarily dismissed SMIC to avoid yet another adverse

11            ruling at her hands (see id. at 11, 18; JRJN Ex. G – CD Cal. Case Dkt. 55 at 3 n.1,

12            11 n.3; JRJN Ex. I – CD Cal. Case Dkt. 63); and

13            (5)    Plaintiff could not voluntarily dismiss SMSC as insinuated in Footnote 1 of

14            the Complaint, only SMIC, because SMSC had secured its own dismissal by

15            establishing ineffectual service (see JRJN Ex. A – CD Cal. Case Dkt. 61 at 12-14).

16            This Court should reject Plaintiff’s thinly veiled gambit to not only take another shot at

17 circumventing due process and/or the Hague Convention as to SMIC and SMSC, but hold Americas

18 liable despite it being an admitted stranger to the purported transaction, all based on the same alter

19 ego allegations and evidence already found lacking by Judge Snyder. Just as in the CD Cal. Case,

20 Plaintiff, at bottom, continues to allege nothing more than that Americas and SMSC are SMIC

21 subsidiaries and, that, as is often the case with parents and subsidiaries, they share a logo and are

22 presented as a single organization on the same website and in documents like annual reports.

23 Compare JRJN Ex. A – CD Cal. Case Dkt. 61 at 4-6 (summarizing jurisdictional facts mustered by

24 Plaintiff) and Complt. ¶¶5, 25-28, 30, 32, 34-40, 42-47, 59, 126-28. And, as Judge Snyder held, and

25 this Court well knows, such insubstantial connections are not enough as a matter of law to

26
     2
27       Both SMSC and SMIC raised alternative grounds for dismissal that Judge Snyder did not reach.

28 See JRJN Ex. A – CD Cal. Case Dkt. 61 at 14, 18.
                                                   2                        Case No. 5:25-cv-04605
                        SMIC, AMERICAS’ NOTICE OF MOTION AND MOTION TO DISMISS;
                                MEMORANDUM OF POINTS AND AUTHORITIES
          Case 5:25-cv-04605-EJD          Document 35        Filed 08/22/25      Page 9 of 17




 1 demonstrate the “pervasive control” and resulting fraud or injustice required to meet the stringent

 2 alter ego test. JRJN Ex. A – CD Cal. Case Dkt. 61 at 16-18; see also, e.g., Ranza v. Nike, Inc., 793

 3 F.3d 1059, 1073 (9th Cir. 2015); Apple v. Allan, 445 F. Supp. 3d 42, 52-55 & n.7 (N.D. Cal. 2020)

 4 (Davila, J.) (rejecting alter ego claim based on far more compelling allegations); Mou v. SSC San

 5 Jose Operating Co. LP, 415 F.Supp.3d 918, 930-931 (N.D. Cal. 2019) (Davila, J.) (same).

 6             Without alter ego, Plaintiff plainly does not have the facts necessary to plausibly state any

 7 claims against Americas, as it otherwise relies exclusively on impermissible group pleading and

 8 allegations confirming that Plaintiff had no interactions of any kind with Americas, only SMIC

 9 representatives and Plaintiff’s former owner, Xing Wang. Indeed, it is this Xing Wang – not

10 Americas – who supposedly aided Plaintiff in placing the alleged Purchase Order, which, on its face,

11 references no one other than Plaintiff and SMSC. See Complt. ¶¶53-72 & Ex. A (Alleged High

12 Sharp Purchase Order, PO No. HSHK211115-001). Count II against Americas is additionally

13 subject to dismissal because the UNCISG does not apply to alleged contracting parties who have

14 their places of business in the same signatory nation, see, e.g., McDowell Valley Vineyards, Inc. v.

15 Sabate USA Inc., No. C-04-0708 SC, 2005 WL 2893848, at *3 (N.D. Cal. Nov. 2, 2005), and the

16 statute of limitations for conversion as asserted in Count IV has run, see Cal. Code of Civil

17 Procedure §338(c)(1).3

18             Accordingly, the Court should dismiss all of Plaintiff’s claims against Americas forthwith.

19 II.         STANDARD OF REVIEW

20             “To survive a motion to dismiss, a complaint must contain sufficient factual matter, accepted

21 as true, to ‘state a claim to relief that is plausible on its face.’” Resh, Inc. v. Skimlite Mfg. Inc., 666

22 F. Supp. 3d 1054, 1058 (N.D. Cal. 2023) (Davila, J.). “A plaintiff must plead factual content that

23 allows the court to draw the reasonable inference that the defendant is liable for the misconduct

24 alleged, which requires more than a sheer possibility that a defendant has acted unlawfully.” Id.

25
     3
26       Americas also joins in the individual arguments against each of Plaintiff’s claims in Sections II(B)-

27 II(E) of the concurrently filed motion to dismiss filed by SMIC (“SMIC MTD”) to the extent

28 applicable.
                                                    3                        Case No. 5:25-cv-04605
                         SMIC, AMERICAS’ NOTICE OF MOTION AND MOTION TO DISMISS;
                                 MEMORANDUM OF POINTS AND AUTHORITIES
      Case 5:25-cv-04605-EJD            Document 35       Filed 08/22/25      Page 10 of 17




 1 (cleaned up). “[T]hreadbare recitals of the elements of a cause of action, supported by mere

 2 conclusory statements, do not suffice.” Id. Further, although the court generally accepts well-pled

 3 allegations as true, it “need not ‘assume the truth of legal conclusions merely because they are cast

 4 in the form of factual allegations.’” Lee v. Plex, 773 F. Supp. 3d 755 (N.D. Cal. 2025). Likewise,

 5 the court need not accept as true allegations that contradict matters properly subject to judicial notice

 6 or documents that are referenced in and central to the complaint. Daniels-Hall v. Nat’l Educ. Ass’n,

 7 629 F.3d 992, 998 (9th Cir. 2010).

 8 III.        ARGUMENT

 9             A.     PLAINTIFF HAS NOT PLAUSIBLY PLED THAT AMERICAS, SMSC, AND
                      SMIC ARE ALTER EGOS
10
               As explained at length infra in Section III.B, Plaintiff does not allege that any defendants
11
     other than SMSC and SMIC were involved in making or breaking the purported semiconductor
12
     wafer deal. See Complt. ¶¶53-72. Rather, Plaintiff seeks to hold Americas (and various DOE
13
     Subsidiaries) liable for SMSC and SMIC’s alleged misconduct on an alter ego theory of liability.
14
     The Complaint, however, does not come remotely close to alleging sufficient facts to invoke the
15
     alter ego doctrine.
16
               To avail itself of this “extreme remedy” that applies “only in exceptional circumstances,”
17
     Apple, 445 F. Supp. 3d at 52, Plaintiff was required to specifically allege with supporting facts that:
18
     (1) “there is such a unity of interest and ownership that the separate personalities of [Americas,
19
     SMSC, and SMIC] no longer exist[]; and (2) “failure to disregard their separate identities would
20
     result in fraud or injustice,” Beluca Ventures LLC v. Aktiebolag, 622 F.Supp.3d 806, 817 (N.D. Cal.
21
     2022). Neither prong was sufficiently pled here. As such, the Court should disregard all of Plaintiff’s
22
     alter ego allegations and dismiss Plaintiff’s claim seeking a declaration that Americas, SMIC, and
23
     SMSC are alter egos (Count VI) as to all defendants.4
24

25
     4
26       Americas also joins in the alter ego arguments in Section I(B)(1)(b) of the SMIC MTD and Section

27 II(A) of Defendant SMSC’s concurrently filed motion to dismiss (“SMSC MTD”) to the extent

28 applicable.
                                                   4                        Case No. 5:25-cv-04605
                        SMIC, AMERICAS’ NOTICE OF MOTION AND MOTION TO DISMISS;
                                MEMORANDUM OF POINTS AND AUTHORITIES
      Case 5:25-cv-04605-EJD           Document 35        Filed 08/22/25      Page 11 of 17




 1                  1.       Plaintiff Has Not Plausibly Pled Fraud or Injustice Would Result

 2          Under the fraud or injustice prong of the alter ego test, a plaintiff must plead sufficient facts

 3 “to support a reasonable inference that there has been ‘an abuse of the corporate privilege’ that

 4 ‘justifies holding the equitable ownership of a corporation liable for the actions of the corporation.’”

 5 Mou, 415 F.Supp.3d at 931. Stated another way, Plaintiff was required to allege sufficient facts to

 6 establish that “conduct amounting to bad faith makes it inequitable for the corporate owner to hide

 7 behind the corporate form.” Perfect 10, Inc. v. Giganews, Inc., 847 F.3d 657, 677 (9th Cir. 2017).

 8 Yet, this it did not even attempt to do. Aside from conclusorily alleging that “[a]dherence to the

 9 fiction of the separate existence of the SMIC, SMSC, SMIC Americas, and the DOE Subsidiaries

10 would permit an abuse of the corporate privilege and would promote injustice and fraud” in

11 Paragraph 131, Plaintiff’s Complaint does not address this prong at all. See Complt. ¶131. This is

12 plainly insufficient, and Plaintiff’s alter ego claim fails on this basis alone. See, e.g., Mou, 415

13 F.Supp.3d at 931 (holding on a motion to dismiss that alter ego claims could not lie even if the unity

14 of interest prong were met, because plaintiff’s “[a]llegations that Defendants operated as a single

15 business for the purpose of ‘lining their pockets with money’ and ‘evad[ing] liability’ and ‘hid[ing]

16 money’ are too vague and conclusory to support a plausible inference that there has been an abuse

17 of corporate privileges” as was his “generalized allegation that all Defendants violated the law”);

18 Apple, 445 F. Supp. 3d at 55 (“Without an allegation addressing this question [of what fraud or

19 injustice will result if the Court declines to find that Defendant A2 is an alter ego of Defendants

20 Allan and/or AAL], Plaintiff has not met its prima facie burden [on the fraud or injustice prong] as

21 to Defendant A2.”); Beluca Ventures, 622 F. Supp. 3d at 817 (rejecting alter ego liability theory

22 where, as here, no attempt was made to specifically plead fraud or injustice).

23                  2.        Plaintiff Has Not Plausibly Pled Unity of Interest

24          Plaintiff has also failed to sufficiently plead facts to meet the “unity of interest and

25 ownership” prong, providing the Court with yet another basis for rejecting its bid to hold Americas

26 liable as an alter ego for SMIC and SMSC. When alter ego liability is predicated on a parent’s
27 (SMIC’s) relationship with its subsidiaries (Americas and SMSC), this prong requires “a showing

28 that the parent controls the subsidiary to such a degree as to render the latter the mere instrumentality
                                                    5                        Case No. 5:25-cv-04605
                         SMIC, AMERICAS’ NOTICE OF MOTION AND MOTION TO DISMISS;
                                 MEMORANDUM OF POINTS AND AUTHORITIES
      Case 5:25-cv-04605-EJD          Document 35        Filed 08/22/25     Page 12 of 17




 1 of the former.” Ranza, 793 F.3d at 1073. It “envisions pervasive control over the subsidiary, such

 2 as when a parent corporation ‘dictates every facet of the subsidiary's business—from broad policy

 3 decisions to routine matters of day-to-day operation.’” Id.

 4          Here, setting aside purely conclusory allegations of unity of interest (Complt. ¶8), all

 5 Plaintiff has alleged as to Americas’ relationships with the other named defendants is that: (i)

 6 Americas is “a wholly owned subsidiary of SMIC” and functions as a SMIC “department” that

 7 markets and sells SMIC products in the United States (id. at ¶¶5, 30, 32, 34-35, 126-127); (ii) SMIC,

 8 SMSC, Americas and the 20 unnamed DOE Subsidiaries publicly “present themselves as a single

 9 company that operates as one,” including by using the word “We” to mean “SMIC and its

10 subsidiaries”; referring to “one SMIC, global operations”; using the “same website,” which lists

11 contact information for Americas, among other SMIC locations; and sharing the same logo (id. at

12 ¶¶ 25-27, 36-40, 42-47, 126-28); (iii) certain SMIC directors and officers purportedly serve as

13 directors or officers of certain unspecified SMIC subsidiaries, without any mention of Americas,

14 other than that in 2018, long before the relevant timeframe for this action, which began in late 2021,

15 a co-CEO of SMIC was identified as CFO and director of Americas (id. ¶¶48–52, 59, 129); and (iv)

16 it was admitted in an answer filed in a different lawsuit in 2017, long before the relevant timeframe

17 for this action, which began in late 2021, that SMIC “controls and is the majority owner[]” of, inter

18 alia, Americas (id. at ¶¶28, 59). But there is a mountain of authority foreclosing Plaintiff’s reliance

19 on these attenuated allegations to make the requisite showing that SMIC “dictates every facet of

20 [Americas and SMSC’s] business.”

21          Courts have repeatedly held that “[t]otal ownership and shared management personnel are

22 alone insufficient to establish the requisite level of control” for unity of interest and ownership.

23 Ranza, 793 F.3d at 1073; Beluca Ventures, 622 F. Supp. 3d at 816; Apple, 445 F.Supp.3d at 53. So

24 too are vague allegations such as those in Paragraph 29 of the Complaint that, Americas’ alleged

25 sole shareholder, SMIC, “controlled” it without any detail as to “how that control was exerted.”

26 Apple, 445 F.Supp.3d at 54-55 & n.7.
27          Mere allegations that subsidiaries used the same trademark as their parent company, or were
